slides.title: Introduction to Scheduling
slides.body: Introduction to Scheduling
slides.notes: First of all we will learn about the Introduction to Scheduling

slides.title: Introduction to Scheduling
slides.body:
What is Scheduling?
When multiple processes want to run, the operating system must decide which one should run next
Processes 1
Processes 2
Processes 3
Operating system
This decision-making is called scheduling
slides.notes: So, let's begin by understanding what scheduling means. Whenever multiple processes are ready to use the CPU, the operating system has to decide which one gets executed next. This process of selecting the next process is called scheduling, and it's essential for efficient CPU utilization.

slides.title: Introduction to Scheduling
slides.body:
Why Scheduling is Needed?
CPU is a limited resource
Many processes are in memory at the same time
Not all can run at once
slides.notes: Now, let's understand why scheduling is necessary. Since the CPU is a limited resource, it can execute only one process at a time. When multiple processes are waiting in memory, scheduling helps the operating system decide the execution order efficiently.

slides.title: Introduction to Scheduling
slides.body:
What It Ensures?
Fair CPU time distribution
Maximizes CPU throughput
Avoids starvation
Minimizes Waiting Time
Minimizes Response Time
Scheduling ensures:
slides.notes: Moving on, scheduling is important because it improves overall system performance. It ensures fair CPU allocation, reduces waiting time, prevents starvation of processes, helps the CPU complete more work in less time, and reduces response times,

slides.title: Scheduler
slides.body:
What Is A Scheduler?
CPU Scheduling
A Scheduler is the OS component that selects which process should run next
Scheduler uses scheduling algorithms (FCFS, SJF, RR, etc.)
slides.notes: Next, let's understand what a scheduler is.It's the operating system component responsible for selecting the next process to run on the CPU. To make this decision, it follows different scheduling algorithms, which we'll explore later in this session.

slides.title: CPU Scheduling
slides.body:
The CPU-I/O Burst Cycle
Execution always begins with a CPU burst and ends with a CPU burst (the final one ends with an exit/termination request)
Process execution is not one continuous stretch of CPU work, it alternates between two phases:
CPU Burst → the process is executing instructions on the CPU
I/O Burst → the process is waiting for an I/O operation (disk, keyboard, network) to finish
slides.notes: Now, let's understand the CPU-I/O burst cycle. A process doesn't use the CPU continuously—it alternates between CPU bursts, where it executes instructions, and I/O bursts, where it waits for input or output operations to complete. This cycle continues until the process finishes, and every process starts and ends with a CPU burst.

slides.title: CPU Scheduling
slides.body:
CPU-Bound Vs I/O-Bound Processes
CPU-bound Process
Spends most time computing
Few, long CPU bursts
Example: video encoding, matrix math
I/O-bound Process
Spends most time waiting on I/O
Many, short CPU bursts
Example: text editor, file copy, web browsing
tables: Spends most time waiting on I/O
Example: text editor, file copy, web browsing
Spends most time waiting on I/O
Example: text editor, file copy, web browsing

slides.title: CPU Scheduling
slides.body:
CPU-Bound Vs I/O-Bound Processes
Most processes have many short CPU bursts and only a few long ones.
A good scheduler mixes CPU-bound and I/O-bound processes so that both the CPU and the I/O devices stay busy at the same time.
This is why scheduling matters: choosing the right process to run keeps the whole system efficient, not just the CPU
slides.notes: Moving on, not all processes use the CPU in the same way. Most processes spend only short periods on the CPU and frequently wait for I/O operations. That's why a good scheduler balances CPU-bound and I/O-bound processes, keeping both the CPU and I/O devices busy. This improves the overall efficiency of the entire system, not just the CPU.

slides.title: Scheduler
slides.body:
Types of Schedulers
To manage processes efficiently, the OS uses three types of Schedulers:
Long-Term Scheduler
Short-Term Scheduler
Medium-Term Scheduler
slides.notes: Next, the operating system uses three types of schedulers to manage processes at different stages. These are the Long-Term, Short-Term, and Medium-Term Schedulers, each serving a specific purpose in process management.

slides.title: Scheduler
slides.body:
Long-Term Scheduler (Job Scheduler)
Decides which processes enter the ready queue
Controls degree of multiprogramming
slides.notes: Now, let's look at the Long-Term Scheduler. It decides which new processes are admitted into the ready queue for execution. By controlling this, it also regulates the degree of multiprogramming in the system.

slides.title: Scheduler
slides.body:
Short-Term Scheduler (CPU Scheduler)
Chooses which ready process runs on CPU next
Most frequent decision-maker
slides.notes: Moving on, the Short-Term Scheduler selects the next process from the ready queue to run on the CPU. Since this decision happens very frequently, it needs to be fast and efficient.

slides.title: Scheduler
slides.body:
Medium-Term Scheduler
Handles swapping (suspend/resume)
Improves memory utilization
slides.notes: Next, the Medium-Term Scheduler manages swapping by temporarily suspending and later resuming processes. This helps free up memory and improves overall memory utilization.

The aim of CPU scheduling is to improve CPU utilization, increase throughput, reduce waiting time, and ensure fairness among processes.

Process Queues in Operating Systems
The OS organizes processes using different queues based on their state
Queues help the scheduler decide which process runs next

Process Queues in Operating Systems

Schedulers & Process Queues
Schedulers operate on Process Queues
Each scheduler has a specific role in process movement
Schedulers
slides.notes: Moving on, schedulers work directly with process queues to manage the movement of processes. Each scheduler performs a specific role, ensuring that processes move efficiently between different states until execution is complete.

slides.title: Process Queues
slides.body:
1 Ready Queue
Contains all processes that are ready to execute
Waiting for CPU allocation
Managed by the CPU scheduler
Processes enter this queue after creation or when they finish I/O
P1
P2
P3
slides.notes: Now, let's begin with the Ready Queue. This queue contains all the processes that are fully prepared to execute but are still waiting for CPU allocation. It's managed by the CPU scheduler, and processes typically enter this queue either right after they're created or after completing an I/O operation.

slides.title: Process Queues
slides.body:
2 Waiting (Blocked) Queue
These processes cannot run until the event occurs
After the event: they move back to Ready Queue
Holds processes that are waiting for some event
I/O completion
Resource availability
Signal/interrupt
slides.notes: Moving on, a process isn't always ready to use the CPU. If it's waiting for an I/O operation to finish, a resource to become available, or a signal or interrupt, it's moved to the Waiting Queue. During this time, it can't execute. Once the event is completed, the process returns to the Ready Queue and waits for CPU allocation.

slides.title: Process Queues
slides.body:
3 Job Queue
Contains all processes in the system
Includes processes waiting to be admitted into memory
Managed by the Long-Term Scheduler (Job Scheduler)
slides.notes:
Next, the Job Queue contains all the processes present in the system,
 including those that are still waiting to be loaded into memory. The Long-Term Scheduler checks this queue and decides which processes should be admitted into memory for execution.

slides.title: Process Queues
slides.body:
4 Device Queues
When I/O is completed → move to Ready Queue
Each I/O device maintains its own queue, contains processes waiting for that particular device
Disk queue
Printer queue
Keyboard queue
slides.notes: Moving on, each I/O device maintains its own Device Queue. So, if a process is waiting to use a disk, printer, or keyboard, it's placed in the corresponding queue. Once the I/O operation is completed, the process moves back to the Ready Queue for execution.

slides.title: CPU Scheduling
slides.body:
What is CPU Scheduling?
CPU Scheduling is the method the OS uses to choose which process gets the CPU next when many are waiting
CPU Scheduling
Processes 1
Processes 2

Operating system
slides.notes: Now, when multiple processes are waiting in the Ready Queue, only one can use the CPU at a time. CPU scheduling is the mechanism the operating system uses to decide which process should get the CPU next.

slides.title: Scheduling Criteria
slides.body:
Definition
Scheduling Criteria are the performance metrics or parameters used to evaluate and compare different CPU Scheduling Algorithms
Scheduling Criteria
slides.notes:
Next, before comparing different scheduling algorithms, we need a way to measure their performance.
 These measures are called scheduling criteria, and they help us evaluate how effectively a scheduling algorithm performs.

slides.title: Scheduling
slides.body:
Benefits
Evaluate how efficiently CPU time is used
Compare scheduling algorithms
Select the right algorithm for system goals
Measure system performance objectively
slides.notes: Moving on, these scheduling criteria help us judge how well a scheduling algorithm performs. They allow us to evaluate CPU utilization, compare different algorithms, choose the one that best fits our system's goals, and measure performance in a fair and objective way

slides.title: Scheduling Criteria
slides.body:
Key Scheduling Criteria
There are five main criteria used to evaluate CPU scheduling algorithms
Each criterion measures a different aspect of scheduling performance
slides.notes: “Tasks mean any operations a computer performs — like calculating numbers, running programs, displaying a webpage, or saving files. Basically, everything you do on a computer is a task handled by both hardware and software together.”

slides.title: Five Key Scheduling Criteria
slides.body:
CPU Utilization
CPU Utilization is the percentage of time the CPU is actively executing processes (not idle)
CPU Utilization Maximize
Goal: Maximize CPU utilization (keep CPU as busy as possible)
slides.notes: Now, let's look at the first scheduling criterion—CPU Utilization. It tells us how much of the time the CPU is actually busy executing processes instead of sitting idle.The objective is to keep the CPU as active as possible and maximize its utilization.

slides.title: Five Key Scheduling Criteria
slides.body:
Throughput
Throughput is the number of processes completed per unit of time
Throughput Maximize
Goal: Maximize throughput (complete more processes in less time)
slides.notes: Next, we have Throughput. It refers to how many processes the system can complete in a given amount of time. A better scheduling algorithm aims to increase throughput by finishing more processes in less time.

slides.title: Five Key Scheduling Criteria
slides.body:
Turnaround Time 
Turnaround Time is the total time taken from process submission to process completion
Turnaround Time Minimize
Goal: Minimize turnaround time(Make processes finish faster)
slides.notes: Moving on, Turnaround Time is the total time a process takes from the moment it's submitted until it finishes execution. The goal is to keep this time as low as possible so that processes complete faster.

slides.title: Five Key Scheduling Criteria
slides.body:
Waiting Time
Waiting Time is the total amount of time a process spends waiting in the Ready Queue before getting CPU time
Waiting Time Minimize
Goal: Minimize waiting time(Reduce waiting as much as possible)
slides.notes: Next, let's look at Waiting Time. This is the total time a process spends waiting in the Ready Queue before it gets CPU time. A good scheduling algorithm tries to minimize this waiting time so processes don't stay in the queue for too long.

slides.title: Five Key Scheduling Criteria
slides.body:
Response Time
Response Time is the time from when a process is submitted until it produces its first response
Response Time Minimize
Goal: Reduce response time, (especially for interactive systems)
slides.notes: Finally, we have Response Time, which focuses on how quickly a process starts responding after it's submitted. This is especially important for interactive applications, where users expect an immediate response, so the goal is to keep this delay as low as possible.

slides.title: Scheduling Criteria
slides.body: Importance of Scheduling Criteria
slides.notes: Now, let's quickly understand why these scheduling criteria matter. Efficient resource utilization ensures the CPU is used effectively. Fairness gives every process a reasonable chance to execute. Responsiveness helps the system react quickly to user requests. And predictability ensures consistent and reliable performance

slides.title: CPU Scheduling
slides.body: CPU Scheduling
slides.notes: Next we will learn about the CPU Scheduling

slides.title: Scheduling Criteria
slides.body:
How Scheduling Works?
Scheduling can operate in two fundamental ways
CPU Scheduling In OS
Non-Preemptive Scheduling
Preemptive Scheduling
These two approaches determine when and how the CPU can be taken away from a running process
slides.notes: Now, let's see how CPU scheduling actually works. Broadly, scheduling follows two approaches: Preemptive and Non-Preemptive. The key difference is whether the operating system can interrupt a running process and assign the CPU to another one.

slides.title: Scheduling Criteria
slides.body:
1. Preemptive Scheduling
In Preemptive Scheduling, the operating system can forcibly take the CPU away from a currently running process and allocate it to another process
Key Characteristic
The operating system has the authority to interrupt a running process, even if the process hasn't completed execution
slides.notes: First, let's understand Preemptive Scheduling. In this approach, the operating system can interrupt a running process whenever needed and assign the CPU to another process. In other words, a process doesn't have to finish its execution before the CPU can be taken away.

slides.title: When Does Preemption Occur?
slides.body:
When Does Preemption Occur?
Preemptive Scheduling
Preemption Conditions: CPU can be taken away when
Higher Priority Process Arrives
Time Quantum Expires
I/O Completion of a Higher-Priority Process
slides.notes: Now, let's see when preemption actually happens. The CPU can be taken away if a higher-priority process arrives, when the assigned time quantum expires, or when an I/O-bound process becomes ready again with a higher priority.

slides.title: When Does Preemption Occur?
slides.body:
When Does Preemption Occur?
Preemptive Scheduling
Preemption Conditions: CPU can be taken away when
A more important process enters Ready Queue
Current process is moved back to Ready Queue
Higher Priority Process Arrives
Time Quantum Expires
I/O Completion of a Higher-Priority Process
slides.notes: Now, let's look at the first situation where preemption occurs. If a higher-priority process enters the Ready Queue, the operating system immediately gives preference to it. As a result, the currently running process is interrupted and moved back to the Ready Queue, allowing the higher-priority process to use the CPU.

slides.title: When Does Preemption Occur?
slides.body:
When Does Preemption Occur?
Preemptive Scheduling
Preemption Conditions: CPU can be taken away when:
Higher Priority Process Arrives:
A more important process enters Ready Queue
Current process is moved back to Ready Queue
Time Quantum Expires:
Process has used its allocated time slice
Must give chance to other processes
System Requirements:
OS needs to respond to urgent events
Better resource utilization needed
Preemption Conditions: CPU can be taken away when
Process has used its allocated time slice
Must give chance to other processes
Higher Priority Process Arrives
Time Quantum Expires
I/O Completion of a Higher-Priority Process
slides.notes: Moving on, another situation where preemption happens is when a process has used up its assigned time quantum. Instead of allowing it to continue, the operating system gives other waiting processes a chance to execute, ensuring fair CPU sharing.

slides.title: When Does Preemption Occur?
slides.body:
When Does Preemption Occur?
Preemptive Scheduling
Preemption Conditions: CPU can be taken away when
OS needs to respond to urgent events
Better resource utilization needed
Higher Priority Process Arrives
Time Quantum Expires
I/O Completion of a Higher-Priority Process
slides.notes: Finally, preemption can also occur when an I/O operation finishes and a higher-priority process becomes ready. In such cases, the operating system quickly switches to that process to respond to urgent events and make better use of system resources.

slides.title: Working
slides.body:
Working
Preemptive Scheduling
Process is selected and allocated CPU
Process begins execution
During execution, OS continuously monitors for:
Timer interrupts (time quantum expired)
Higher priority process arrivals
I/O completion of a higher-priority process
Process Flow
slides.notes: Now, let's see how preemptive scheduling works. A process is first selected and given the CPU to execute. While it's running, the operating system continuously checks for events like a timer interrupt, the arrival of a higher-priority process, or the completion of I/O for a higher-priority process. If any of these occur, the CPU may be reassigned immediately.

slides.title: Working
slides.body:
Working
Preemptive Scheduling
If preemption condition occurs:
Current process is interrupted
Process state is saved (context switching)
Process moves back to Ready Queue
Next process is scheduled
Original process waits for next CPU allocation
slides.notes: If any of these conditions are met, the running process is interrupted, and its current state is saved through context switching. The process is then moved back to the Ready Queue, another eligible process gets the CPU, and the interrupted process waits for its next turn to execute.

slides.title: Analogy
slides.body:
Analogy
1. Preemptive Scheduling
How Non-Preemptive Scheduling Works
Process Flow:
Process is selected from Ready Queue by scheduler
CPU is allocated to the process
Process executes continuously
Process runs until one of these occurs:
Completion: Process finishes execution
I/O Request: Process needs input/output operation
Voluntary Wait: Process enters waiting state
Only then does the next process get CPU
Now picture a doctor treating patients. She's in the middle of a routine checkup when an accident victim is rushed in. She immediately pauses the checkup, attends to the emergency, and returns to the first patient afterward. The current patient doesn't get to finish just because they started — a more urgent case (higher priority) or a strict time limit can force the doctor to switch.

slides.title: Advantages
slides.body:
Advantages
Preemptive Scheduling
Better Responsiveness
Fair CPU Sharing
Suitable for Real-Time Systems
slides.notes: let's look at the advantages of preemptive scheduling. Better responsiveness allows the system to react quickly to important tasks, fair CPU sharing ensures every process gets a chance to execute, and it's well-suited for real-time systems, where timely execution is critical.

slides.title: Disadvantages
slides.body:
Disadvantages
Preemptive Scheduling
Common scheduling algorithms that use preemptive approach
More Overhead
Complex to Implement
Possible Starvation
slides.notes: On the other hand, preemptive scheduling also has a few drawbacks. More overhead is caused by frequent context switching, implementation is more complex because the OS must constantly monitor running processes, and starvation can occur if lower-priority processes keep getting postponed.

slides.body:

slides.title: 2. Non-Preemptive Scheduling
slides.body:
2. Non-Preemptive Scheduling
Scheduling Criteria
In Non-Preemptive Scheduling, once the CPU is allocated to a process, that process keeps the CPU until it either
Definition
Completes its execution (terminates), OR
Voluntarily releases the CPU (e.g., for I/O operation)
Key Characteristic: The operating system cannot forcibly take the CPU away from a running process
slides.notes: Now, let's look at Non-Preemptive Scheduling. In this approach, once a process gets the CPU, it continues executing until it either completes its execution or voluntarily gives up the CPU, such as while waiting for an I/O operation. Unlike preemptive scheduling, the operating system cannot interrupt a running process.

slides.title: Working
slides.body:
Working
2. Non-Preemptive Scheduling
Process is selected from Ready Queue by scheduler
CPU is allocated to the process
Process executes continuously
Process Flow
slides.notes: Next, let's understand how it works. The scheduler first selects a process from the Ready Queue and allocates the CPU to it. Once execution begins, the process continues running without interruption until it finishes or releases the CPU on its own.

slides.title: Working
slides.body:
Working
2. Non-Preemptive Scheduling
Process runs until one of these occurs:
Completion: Process finishes execution
I/O Request: Process needs input/output operation
Voluntary Wait: Process enters waiting state
Only then does the next process get CPU
Process Flow
slides.notes: After that, the process keeps running until it either completes its execution, requests an I/O operation, or voluntarily enters the waiting state. Only after one of these events does the scheduler select the next process for execution.

slides.title: Analogy
slides.body:
Analogy
2. Non-Preemptive Scheduling
Picture people lined up at an ATM. Once someone steps up and starts their transaction, they use the machine until they're completely done — checking balance, withdrawing cash, printing receipt. Even if the person behind them is in a huge rush, they must wait. The machine is handed over only when the current user finishes and walks away on their own. Control is given up voluntarily.
slides.notes: Consider an ATM.Once someone steps up and starts their transaction, they use the machine until they're completely done — checking balance, withdrawing cash, printing receipt. Even if the person behind them is in a huge rush, they must wait. The machine is handed over only when the current user finishes and walks away on their own.

slides.title: Advantages
slides.body:
Advantages
2. Non-Preemptive Scheduling
Simple to Implement
No Overhead of Frequent Switching
Predictable Execution
slides.notes: Moving on, non-preemptive scheduling offers a few key advantages. Predictable execution lets a process run without interruption, it's simpler to implement since the scheduler makes fewer decisions, and it avoids frequent context switching, reducing scheduling overhead.

slides.title: Disadvantages
slides.body:
Disadvantages
2. Non-Preemptive Scheduling
Poor Response Time
Risk of Long Waiting Times
Poor Responsiveness to Urgent Processes
slides.notes: However, non-preemptive scheduling has some limitations. Urgent processes may have to wait, leading to poor response time, and if a long process gets the CPU first, other processes might experience long waiting times before they can execute.

slides.title: Dispatcher
slides.body:
Introduction
The dispatcher is the OS module that actually hands the CPU over to the process chosen by the short-term scheduler
The scheduler decides; the dispatcher does
slides.notes:
Now, let's understand the role of the Dispatcher. 
Once the short-term scheduler decides which process should run next, the dispatcher takes over and actually transfers the CPU to that process. In simple terms, the scheduler decides, and the dispatcher executes that decision.

slides.notes: Moving on, dispatcher performs three important tasks on every switch:after the scheduler selects a process, the dispatcher makes sure it's ready to run &restores the process's previously saved state, switches the CPU from kernel mode to user mode, and then transfers control to the appropriate instruction so the process can either resume from where it stopped or start executing.

Callout box (Scheduler vs Dispatcher):
slides.notes: Now, it's important not to confuse the scheduler with the dispatcher. The scheduler acts as the brain by deciding which process should run next, while the dispatcher acts as the hands by carrying out that decision and giving the CPU to the selected process.

slides.title: Dispatcher
slides.body:
Dispatch Latency
Dispatch latency = the time the dispatcher takes to stop one process and start another running.
It includes: context switch time + mode switch time + time to jump to the program
The dispatcher runs during every single process switch, so it must be as fast as possible.
Lower dispatch latency → higher CPU efficiency (less time wasted between processes)
slides.notes: Finally, every time the CPU switches from one process to another, the dispatcher takes a small amount of time to complete the switch. This includes saving and restoring process information, switching to user mode, and transferring control to the new process. Since this happens during every process switch,lower dispatch latency means less CPU time is wasted and overall system efficiency improves.

slides.title: Gantt Chart
slides.body:
Introduction
A Gantt chart is a horizontal bar chart that shows which process is using the CPU at each point in time.
X-axis = time. Each bar = one process running during that time interval
We use it to visualize the schedule and to calculate completion time, turnaround time, and waiting time
slides.notes: Now, before we study the scheduling algorithms, let's understand the Gantt Chart. It's a horizontal chart where the X-axis represents time, and each bar represents the process running during that time interval. It helps us visualize the execution sequence and calculate important metrics like completion time, turnaround time, and waiting time.
